title: Nurse Lillian Wald brought care to immigrant homes in New York and founded Henry Street

trailer.text: Lillian Wald, a Jewish nurse from Cincinnati, coined the term public health nurse.
On New York's Lower East Side, residents of the crowded tenements were frequently sick.
In 1893 Wald, together with Mary Brewster, established the Visiting Nurses Service there.
The nurses came to homes on referrals from physicians and patients, and charged fees only to those who could pay.
From this grew the Henry Street Settlement, which today runs more than 50 programs in health care, social services and the arts.

glance.label: Where
glance.value: 265 Henry Street, Lower East Side, New York

glance.label: Scale today
glance.value: About 50,000 people a year, according to Wikipedia

glance.label: Recognition
glance.value: Hall of Fame of Great Americans, 1965

paragraphs.text: Lillian D. Wald was born on March 10, 1867, in Cincinnati, Ohio.
She was the second daughter and third of four children of Max D. Wald and Minnie Schwarz Wald.
She was born to a Jewish family and had a childhood of privilege.
She received no Jewish education and was raised in a liberal Jewish atmosphere.
At sixteen she applied to Vassar College.
She was refused because of her age.
The sources give two accounts of what led Wald to choose nursing.
In 1889 she enrolled in the nursing program of the New York Hospital training school.
After graduating in 1891, she worked as a nurse at the New York Juvenile Asylum.
She quickly became disillusioned with institutional methods of caring for children.
In 1892 she enrolled at the Women's Medical College in New York.

stations.title: The most crowded neighborhood in the world

paragraphs.text: According to Aish, by 1900 the Lower East Side was the most crowded neighborhood in the world, with more than 700 residents per acre.
It was not unusual for a family of ten to live there in an apartment of about 325 square feet.
Because of the crowding, and because no one maintained the buildings, residents were frequently sick.
At the beginning of the 20th century, thousands of Eastern European Jews lived in these tenements.
When Wald began her work, there were no city public health nurses in New York.

According to the Encyclopedia of World Biography, the needs of the immigrants were great and the medical care available to them was slight, to the point that Wald abandoned her career and in 1893 moved with another student to live on the East Side.

stations.title: The girl who asked for help

paragraphs.text: Wald taught home health care to women from immigrant families on the Lower East Side.
One day, in the middle of a class, a little girl asked her to attend to her sick mother.
With funding from philanthropists and friends, Wald and Mary Brewster established the Visiting Nurses Service in 1893.
By January 1894 the two had visited more than 125 families and advised many more.
According to the encyclopedia, wealthy Jews who felt a duty to their coreligionists in the slums helped Wald from the start.
Betty Loeb, who had funded the nursing classes, and her son-in-law, the banker and philanthropist Jacob Henry Schiff, gave Wald the money to move to 265 Henry Street.
There the Henry Street Settlement House was founded.
According to the Social Welfare History Project at Virginia Commonwealth University, the work of Lillian Wald, together with Mary Brewster, began in July 1893.
Wald gave the name public health nurses to nurses who worked outside hospitals, in poor and middle-class communities.
According to Aish, she was the one who coined the term public health nursing.
The nurses responded to referrals from physicians and patients, and received fees based on what the patient could pay.
The sliding fee scale was meant to give all city residents access to medical attention.
Wald resolved early that the Henry Street nurses would be nonsectarian, and that only those who could pay would pay.
The service grew to many centers and many buildings.
According to the National Women's History Museum, in 1913 the Henry Street Settlement House had 3,000 members in its classes and clubs.
According to another biographical entry on Encyclopedia.com, Wald did more than any other individual to invent and popularize the American version of public health nursing.

stations.title: Beyond nursing: children, labor and equality

paragraphs.text: One of Henry Street's first projects was to turn the house's small backyard into a playground.
The Outdoor Recreation League, which Wald helped found, raised funds to improve Seward Park, which later became the first municipal playground in New York City.
Wald also led campaigns for parks, better housing and the elimination of tuberculosis.
In 1900 she convinced the New York City Board of Education to hire Elizabeth Farrell, a Henry Street resident, to teach special education classes.
In 1902 she succeeded in having Lina L. Rogers, a Henry Street nurse, hired as New York City's first public school nurse.
In her first month, Rogers treated 893 students, made 137 home visits and helped 25 children return to school.
Wald also established a scholarship that allowed talented boys and girls to remain in school until age sixteen.
According to NewYork-Presbyterian, Wald ensured that all classes at Henry Street were racially integrated.
She was a founding member of the NAACP, and before that the National Negro Committee held its first conference in 1909 at Henry Street.
According to Aish, in 1906 Wald hired a Black nurse for the first time.
Wald and members of a commission traveled 1,286 miles in fourteen days to investigate the working conditions of immigrants at highway and canal camps.
Their report led to the formation of a State Bureau of Industries in New York.
In 1903 she helped found the Women's Trade Union League,
and in 1909 Henry Street and the Metropolitan Life company became partners in an effort to provide health care to workers.
She also worked for the creation of the Federal Children's Bureau.
In 1912 the National Organization for Public Health Nursing chose her as its first president.

According to JWA, Wald headed the Red Cross Nurses' Emergency Council, which was established in response to the 1918 influenza epidemic, and under her direction Henry Street "cleared all cases of influenza" and mobilized the efforts of thousands of volunteers.
In 1922 the New York Times named her one of the twelve greatest living American women.
Toward the end of her career, Wald retired from running Henry Street.
She died in Westport on September 1, 1940, at age seventy-three, after a long illness brought on by a cerebral hemorrhage.
In 1965 she was elected to the Hall of Fame of Great Americans at New York University.
Today the Henry Street Settlement remains a fixture of the Lower East Side, with more than 50 programs in health care, social services and the arts.
According to Wikipedia, it serves about 50,000 people each year.
In 1915 Wald was elected president of the American Union Against Militarism, founded that same year.
As war drew nearer, her position cost Henry Street some of its funding.
The sources disagree on what she did when the United States joined the war.
In 1919, in the wake of the American reaction to the rise of communism, her name was listed with 61 others in a document presented to the judiciary.
Historians have criticized the settlement house movement, which, they say, forced expectations and behaviors on immigrant communities.
According to the encyclopedia, Wald's books do not reveal her inner life and do not explain the dynamics of American society.

disagreements.question: What led Wald to study nursing?

versions.says: According to JWA, she was present at the birth of her sister Julia's child, and was so impressed by the nurse's work that she decided to become a nurse
According to the National Women's History Museum, in 1889 she met a young nurse who inspired her

disagreements.question: Which nursing school did Wald attend?

versions.says: According to JWA, the New York Hospital training school for nurses, where she enrolled in 1889
According to the Encyclopedia of World Biography, the School of Nursing at Bellevue Hospital, from which she graduated in 1891

disagreements.question: Did Wald see her work as helping her fellow Jews?

versions.says: According to Aish, Wald knew she had to create new public health resources to help her fellow Jews
According to JWA, Wald expressed no particular religious connection between herself and the Jewish immigrants she worked with

disagreements.question: In what year did Wald begin teaching on the Lower East Side?

versions.says: According to Wikipedia, in 1892 she volunteered to teach a class on home health care for immigrant women
According to NewYork-Presbyterian, in 1893, at age 25, she was asked to teach home nursing to immigrant families

disagreements.question: In what year was Wald's settlement house founded?

versions.says: According to Wikipedia, in 1893, under the name Nurses' Settlement

According to My Jewish Learning, Wald and Mary Brewster established the Visiting Nurses Service in 1893 with funding from philanthropists and friends, and "One year later", in the site's words, Wald moved to 265 Henry Street and founded the Henry Street Settlement House.
According to the National Women's History Museum, in 1894
According to JWA, in 1895

disagreements.question: In what year did the service have eighteen nursing centers?

versions.says: According to Women of Valor, by 1903 eighteen centers treated 4,500 patients a year
According to the JWA encyclopedia, in 1905 alone there were eighteen centers and 4,500 patients

disagreements.question: How many buildings did the organization have in 1913?

versions.says: According to the National Women's History Museum, seven buildings on Henry Street and two satellite centers
According to the Encyclopedia of World Biography, nine houses, seven vacation homes in the country and three stores used as stock rooms, milk stations and clinics

disagreements.question: How many nurses did the organization employ?

versions.says: According to the National Women's History Museum, 92 nurses who made about 200,000 home visits a year
According to the Encyclopedia of World Biography, 100 nurses by 1914
According to Aish, 265 nurses who cared for 100,000 patients by the time she retired in 1933

disagreements.question: When did Wald begin working for the Children's Bureau?

versions.says: According to Women of Valor, she conceived of the bureau in 1905
According to JWA, she worked for its creation from 1906 until 1912

disagreements.question: When did Wald retire from running Henry Street?

versions.says: According to the National Women's History Museum, in 1930, when she became Director Emeritus
According to JWA, in 1933, when she retired to her house in Westport, Connecticut

disagreements.question: How many people attended the memorial?

versions.says: According to Women of Valor, 2,500 people filled Carnegie Hall a few months after her death to hear messages from the president, the governor and the mayor
According to Aish, more than 2,000 people, including the Mayor of New York City and the Governor of the State

disagreements.question: Did Wald hold to her pacifism even when the United States went to war?

versions.says: According to JWA, she held fast to her pacifism even when some contributors protested and withdrew their support
According to Women of Valor, after the United States joined the war she abandoned her stance

claims.text: וולד וחברי הוועדה נסעו 1286 מייל בארבעה עשר יום כדי לחקור תנאי עבודה של מהגרים במחנות כבישים ותעלות.
claims.quote: Wald and the other commission members traveled 1286 miles in fourteen days to investigate working conditions among immigrant laborers at highway and canal project camps.

claims.text: דוח הוועדה, שדרש שיפור תנאי המחיה והעבודה של העובדים ומשפחותיהם, הוביל להקמת לשכה מדינתית לתעשיות בניו יורק.
claims.quote: which called for the creation of improved living and working standards for the workers and their families, led to the formation of a State Bureau of Industries in New York

claims.text: ב-1903 סייעה וולד להקים את ליגת האיגודים המקצועיים של נשים כדי לחקור את תנאי עבודתן של נשים ולקדם איגודים.
claims.quote: In 1903, she helped found the WTUL to investigate women's working conditions and promote the creation of women's trade unions.

claims.text: ב-1909 הפכו הנרי סטריט וחברת מטרופוליטן לייף לשותפות במאמץ לספק טיפול רפואי איכותי לעובדים.
claims.quote: In 1909, Henry Street and Metropolitan Life became partners in an effort to provide quality health care to employed workers.

claims.text: לפי Women of Valor, וולד הגתה את לשכת הילדים הפדרלית ב-1905 וחירפה נפשה למענה.
claims.quote: Wald conceived of the Federal Children's Bureau in 1905 and campaigned for it tirelessly.

claims.text: לפי JWA, וולד עבדה ללא לאות להקמת לשכת הילדים מ-1906 עד 1912.
claims.quote: and worked unceasingly for its creation from 1906 until 1912

claims.text: הארגון הלאומי לסיעוד בריאות הציבור בחר בוולד כנשיאתו הראשונה ב-1912.
claims.quote: The National Organization for Public Health Nursing, an association for a profession she herself had founded, chose Wald as its first president in 1912.

claims.text: לפי JWA, תחת הנחייתה טיפלה הנרי סטריט בכל מקרי השפעת וגייסה אלפי מתנדבים.
claims.quote: Under her direction, Henry Street cleared all cases of influenza and mobilized the efforts of thousands of volunteers.

claims.text: ב-1922 בחר הניו יורק טיימס בוולד כאחת משתים עשרה הנשים האמריקאיות החיות הגדולות ביותר.
claims.quote: In 1922, the New York Times named Wald one of the 12 greatest living American women.

claims.text: לפי המוזיאון הלאומי להיסטוריה של נשים, ב-1930 פרשה וולד והפכה למנהלת אמריטה של הנרי סטריט.
claims.quote: In 1930, Wald retired and became the Director Emeritus for the Henry Street Settlement.

claims.text: לפי JWA, ב-1933 התפטרה וולד מתפקיד ראש הצוות ופרשה לביתה בווסטפורט, קונטיקט.
claims.quote: In 1933, she resigned as headworker of Henry Street Settlement and retired to her house-on-the-pond in Westport, Connecticut.

claims.text: וולד מתה בווסטפורט ב-1 בספטמבר 1940, בגיל שבעים ושלוש, לאחר מחלה ממושכת שנגרמה משטף דם מוחי.
claims.quote: Lillian Wald died in Westport on September 1, 1940, at age seventy-three, after a long illness brought on by a cerebral hemorrhage.

claims.text: לפי Women of Valor, כמה חודשים אחרי מותה מילאו 2,500 איש את קרנגי הול לשמוע מסרים מהנשיא, מהמושל ומראש העיר.
claims.quote: A few months later, 2,500 people filled Carnegie Hall to hear messages from the president, governor, mayor, and others

claims.text: לפי Aish, מעל 2,000 איש השתתפו באזכרה, ובהם ראש עיריית ניו יורק ומושל המדינה.
claims.quote: Over 2,000 people attended her memorial service, including the Mayor of New York City and the Governor of New York State.

claims.text: ב-1915 נבחרה וולד לנשיאת האיגוד האמריקאי נגד מיליטריזם שהוקם זה עתה.
claims.quote: In 1915, she was elected president of the newly formed American Union Against Militarism

claims.text: ככל שהתלהטה להט המלחמה, עמדתה האנטי-מיליטריסטית של וולד עלתה להנרי סטריט בחלק ממימונו.
claims.quote: as war fervor intensified, Wald's anti-militarist position cost Henry Street some of its funding

claims.text: לפי JWA, וולד נצמדה לפציפיזם שלה גם כשחלק מהתורמים להנרי סטריט מחו ומשכו תמיכה.
claims.quote: She held fast to her pacifism even when some contributors to Henry Street protested her platform and withdrew support.

claims.text: לפי Women of Valor, לאחר שארצות הברית הצטרפה למלחמה זנחה וולד את עמדתה האנטי-מיליטריסטית.
claims.quote: After the U.S. joined the war, Wald abandoned her anti-militarist stance but remained affiliated with the Foreign Policy Organization

claims.text: ב-1919, בעקבות התגובה האמריקאית לעליית הקומוניזם, נכללה וולד עם 61 אחרים במסמך שהוגש לרשות השיפוטית.
claims.quote: In 1919, however, in the wake of the American reaction to the rise of communism, Wald, with sixty-one other women and men, was listed in a document presented to the U.S. Judiciary

claims.text: היסטוריונים מתחו ביקורת על תנועת בתי הקהילה על שהטילה ציפיות והתנהגויות על קהילות מהגרים.
claims.quote: Historians have since critiqued the settlement house movement for the ways in which it forced certain expectations and behaviors on immigrant communities.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה, ספריה של וולד אינם חושפים את חייה הפנימיים ואינם מסבירים את הדינמיקה של החברה האמריקאית.
claims.quote: Although her books do not reveal her innermost life and do not explain the dynamics of American society

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה העולמית לביוגרפיה, וולד סיימה ב-1891 את בית הספר לסיעוד של בית החולים בלווי בניו יורק.
claims.quote: In 1891 she graduated from the School of Nursing at Bellevue Hospital in New York City.

claims.text: לפי Aish, וולד ידעה שעליה לעשות שינוי ולהקים משאבי בריאות ציבור חדשים כדי לעזור לבני עמה היהודים.
claims.quote: Lillian knew she had to make a difference, creating major new public health resources to help her fellow Jews.

claims.text: לפי JWA, וולד לא הביעה קשר דתי מיוחד בינה לבין המהגרים היהודים שעבדה איתם.
claims.quote: She expressed no particular religious connection between herself and the Jewish immigrants with whom she worked

claims.text: לפי ויקיפדיה, הארגון נוסד ב-1893 בשם Nurses' Settlement על ידי וולד.
claims.quote: It was founded under the name Nurses' Settlement in 1893 by progressive reformer and nurse Lillian Wald.

claims.text: לפי המוזיאון הלאומי להיסטוריה של נשים, ב-1894 וולד וברוסטר הקימו את הנרי סטריט סטלמנט.
claims.quote: In 1894, Wald and Brewster started the Henry Street Settlement House, an organization dedicated to providing social services

claims.text: לפי JWA, ב-1895 עברה וולד לרחוב הנרי 265 והקימה שם את בית הקהילה של האחיות.
claims.quote: In 1895, Wald took up residence at 265 Henry Street where she founded the

claims.text: לפי Women of Valor, עד 1903 שמונה עשר מוקדי סיעוד טיפלו ב-4500 מטופלים בשנה.
claims.quote: By 1903, eighteen district nursing service centers treated 4500 patients a year.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה העולמית לביוגרפיה, עד 1913 היו בבעלות הארגון תשעה בתים, שבעה בתי נופש בכפר ושלוש חנויות ששימשו כמחסנים, תחנות חלב ומרפאות.
claims.quote: By 1913 it owned nine houses, seven vacation homes in the country, and three stores used as stock rooms, milk stations, clinics

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה העולמית לביוגרפיה, עד 1914 עבדו 100 אחיות מתוך בית האחיות.
claims.quote: 100 nurses were working out of what was then called the Nurses' Settlement by 1914

claims.text: לפי Aish, בזמן פרישתה ב-1933 העסיק הארגון 265 אחיות שטיפלו ב-100,000 מטופלים.
claims.quote: By the time she retired in 1933, the organization she led employed 265 nurses who cared for 100,000 patients.

claims.text: לפי פרויקט ההיסטוריה של הרווחה החברתית באוניברסיטת וירג'יניה קומנוולת', הפעילות של ליליאן וולד, יחד עם מרי ברוסטר, החלה ביולי 1893.
claims.quote: July, 1893, by Lillian D. Wald
